name: Human-like Memory Recall and Consolidation

paper.title: "My agent understands me better": Integrating Dynamic Human-like Memory Recall and Consolidation in LLM-Based Agents

construction.unit: event: a short statement about the user (e.g. "User stayed at home") with its time
construction.kept_as: short event sentences derived from the chat history; how they are generated is not described
construction.processing: chat events generated from the dialogue history and embedded into a vector store (details not given)

organization.structure: flat event store + raw chat history
organization.stores: Qdrant vector store of events (content, time, recall strength g); Firestore chat history
organization.index: dense vectors, cosine similarity (embedding model not stated)

management.operations: on each recall the event's decay slows: g_n = g_(n-1) + S(t), S(t) = (1 - e^-t)/(1 + e^-t)
management.forgetting: none by design: recall probability decays with time but never reaches zero

retrieval.selection: recall probability p_n(t) from cosine relevance r, elapsed time t and strength g_n; recall when p exceeds k = 0.86
retrieval.budget: one past dialogue history / event added to the prompt

use.context: agent persona prompt, system prompt with the user's schedule and current time, plus the recalled event

classify.note: Selection is a fixed formula plus a threshold (p > 0.86), with one event passed on; the only update is the recall-strength counter g of a recalled event. How events are written is not described.

stages.ingestion: Chat turns are kept in a Firestore chat history; an EventHandler builds chat events from past dialogue (the paper gives no prompt or rule for this).
stages.construction: Each event is a short sentence about the user (e.g. "User went to the university today") stored in Qdrant with its time and a recall strength g that starts at 1.
stages.organization: One flat vector collection of events alongside the raw chat history.
stages.update: When an event is recalled, its g grows by S(t) = (1 - e^-t)/(1 + e^-t), which is larger for longer gaps since the last recall, so the event decays more slowly afterwards; nothing is deleted.
stages.retrieval: The user's message is embedded; each candidate event gets p_n(t) = (1 - exp(-r e^(-t/g_n)))/(1 - e^-1) with r the cosine similarity and t the elapsed time, and is recalled when p exceeds 0.86.
stages.answer: GPT-4-0613 answers with a persona prompt, a system prompt holding the current time and the user's schedule, and a single recalled past dialogue.

summary: Dialogue-agent memory that recalls a past event only when a cognitive-psychology recall probability (relevance x time decay, slowed by each spaced recall) passes a threshold, instead of summing recency, importance and relevance scores.
notes: Venue: CHI 2024 Late-Breaking Work, published in the Extended Abstracts (CHI EA '24, Honolulu, 7 pages, DOI 10.1145/3613905.3650839; ACM reference in the PDF and dx.doi.org page). Track set to 'short' (extended abstract), not 'main'. Text read from arXiv v1. No code link in the paper and none found by web search; everything here is from the 7-page paper. Construction details (how events are generated, embedding model, time units) are not given, so those design fields are null. The per-task losses come from the bar labels of Fig. 3-A.

sources.code_note: No official code: the paper gives no repository link, and a web search found only unrelated projects. Everything is taken from the paper; the implementation of event generation, the embedding model and the time units of t cannot be checked.

headline: The recall score is a formula, not a learned or prompted choice: cosine relevance decayed by elapsed time, with slower decay for events recalled at long intervals.
Only one past event or dialogue enters the prompt, and only when its recall probability passes 0.86.
The evaluation is 10 hand-built recall tasks with 4 candidate events each, scored against Generative Agents' scoring rule; no public benchmark is used.

GPT-4-0613 with persona and time prompts plus one recalled past dialogue

answer_context.sees: persona prompt, system prompt with the user's schedule and the current time, and one retrieved past dialogue
answer_context.format: not given beyond the two prompt texts in §6
includes: at most one recalled past dialogue / event

compression.what: recalled items in the prompt vs stored events
compression.basis: Not reported as a ratio: §5 says only one past dialogue history is added, and the store size is not given.

numbers.label: Loss vs Generative Agents
numbers.value: lower on 10 of 10 tasks; t = -5.687, p = 0.000299

open_questions: The table scores (e.g. Table 1: 0.850 for r 0.776, t 434,700 s, g 5.102) cannot be reproduced with Eq. 8 for any single time unit we tried (seconds to years), so the scaling of t is unclear.
Several recalls in Tables 1 and 3 have scores below 0.86 (0.850, 0.772), so the evaluation seems to take the top-scoring event rather than apply the threshold.

text: Past dialogue is kept in Firestore and turned into short events about the user, each stored in Qdrant with its time and a recall strength g that starts at 1.
Every time an event is recalled, g grows (more for longer gaps), so the event fades more slowly; nothing is ever deleted.

text: Candidate events are scored by a recall probability that combines cosine relevance, elapsed time and recall strength.
An event whose probability passes 0.86 is added to GPT-4's prompt and consolidated; at most one past dialogue is used.

components.model: Qdrant vector search (embedding model not stated)

discussion.takeaway: Replacing a weighted recency/importance/relevance score with a recall-probability model in which spaced recalls slow forgetting picks the expected event in 9 of 10 small hand-built tasks where Generative Agents' scoring picks 1.

claims.claim: Lower recall loss than Generative Agents' scoring.
claims.evidence: Loss lower on all 10 tasks (e.g. 0.200 vs 0.500 on task 1); paired t = -5.687, p = 0.000299, 95% CI of the difference [-0.27, -0.12]. Fig. 3, §4.2

claims.claim: The agent's replies reflect recalled user habits and preferences.
claims.evidence: Two dialogue examples from the user study (ice cream reward, Hawaii paper deadline). Tables 3-4, §4.3.1
Only one past dialogue is added to the prompt. §5

limits: Relies on long-term behaviour patterns, so it adapts poorly when the user's habits change (e.g. Task 0, where both models fail).
Needs a larger, high-quality dataset; the combination of relevance, time and frequency is not tuned.
Storage and compute costs of the database interaction are not studied.
Evaluated on specific domains and tasks only.
reading: The quantitative test is 10 tasks built from the authors' own conversation logs, each asking which of 4 events should be recalled; the loss compares softmax-normalised scores with a one-hot label, not answer quality.
The comparison changes only the scoring rule: Generative Agents' recency, importance and relevance scores are recomputed on the same events, with importance values (2-7) whose source is not stated.
The threshold 0.86 is set by trial, and scores below it are still counted as recalls in the examples, so the trigger itself is not evaluated.
The time unit inside Eq. 8 is not stated, and the reported scores do not follow Eq. 8 with t in any single unit we tried.
No code, embedding model or event-generation prompt is given, and the user study reports two example dialogues and no measured outcome.

abstract.text: The paper gives an LLM dialogue agent a memory modelled on human cued recall and consolidation. Past events about the user are kept in a vector database with their time, and a recall probability built from cosine relevance and elapsed time decides whether an event is brought back. Each recall slows the event's future decay, more so when recalls are spaced out, and memories never fully disappear. On 10 small recall tasks the model has lower loss than Generative Agents' scoring, and a short user study shows replies that use recalled preferences.
abstract.note: Summary in our words; the original abstract is on arXiv.
